fetched_contents.text: Classify Your Medical Device UPDATE: December 5, 2025 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is requesting public comment on existing medical device accessories that may or may not be suitable for distinct classification in Class I. This request for public comment is a preliminary step to help the FDA identify suitable accessories for distinct classification into Class I and is intended to seek early feedback from groups and individuals outside the Agency. The FDA intends to consider all relevant comments submitted within 90 days, on or before March 5, 2026, to develop a proposal for the distinct classification action. * After initially issuing the Request for Public Comment, the FDA extended the comment period by 30 days. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has established classifications for approximately 1,700 different generic types of devices and grouped them into 16 medical specialties referred to as panels. Each of these generic types of devices is assigned to one of three regulatory classes based on the level of control necessary to assure the safety and effectiveness of the device. The three classes and the requirements which apply to them are: Device Class and Regulatory Controls 1. Class I General Controls * With Exemptions * Without Exemptions 2. Class II General Controls and Special Controls * With Exemptions * Without Exemptions 3. Class III General Controls and Premarket Approval The class to which your device is assigned determines, among other things, the type of premarketing submission/application required for FDA clearance to market. If your device is classified as Class I or II, and if it is not exempt, a 510k will be required for marketing. All devices classified as exempt are subject to the limitations on exemptions. Limitations of device exemptions are covered under 21 CFR xxx.9, where xxx refers to Parts 862-892. For Class III devices, a premarket approval application (PMA) will be required unless your device is a preamendments device (on the market prior to the passage of the medical device amendments in 1976, or substantially equivalent to such a device) and PMA's have not been called for. In that case, a 510k will be the route to market. Device classification depends on the intended use of the device and also upon indications for use. For example, a scalpel's intended use is to cut tissue. A subset of intended use arises when a more specialized indication is added in the device's labeling such as, "for making incisions in the cornea". Indications for use can be found in the device's labeling, but may also be conveyed orally during sale of the product. A discussion of the meaning of intended use is contained in The 510(k) Program: Evaluating Substantial Equivalence in Premarket Notification [510(k)]. In addition, classification is risk based, that is, the risk the device poses to the patient and/or the user is a major factor in the class it is assigned. Class I includes devices with the lowest risk and Class III includes those with the greatest risk. As indicated above all classes of devices as subject to General Controls. General Controls are the baseline requirements of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act that apply to all medical devices, Class I, II, and III. How to Determine Classification To find the classification of your device, as well as whether any exemptions may exist, you need to find the regulation number that is the classification regulation for your device. There are two methods for accomplishing this: go directly to the classification database and search for a part of the device name, or, if you know the device panel (medical specialty) to which your device belongs, go directly to the listing for that panel and identify your device and the corresponding regulation. You may make a choice now, or continue to read the background information below. If you continue to read, you will have another chance to go to these destinations. If you already know the appropriate panel you can go directly to the CFR and find the classification for your device by reading through the list of classified devices, or if you're not sure, you can use the keyword directory in the PRODUCT CODE CLASSIFICATION DATABASE. In most cases this database will identify the classification regulation in the CFR. You can also check the classification regulations below for information on various products and how they are regulated by CDRH. Each classification panel in the CFR begins with a list of devices classified in that panel. Each classified device has a 7-digit number associated with it, e.g., 21 CFR 880.2920 - Clinical Mercury Thermometer. Once you find your device in the panel's beginning list, go to the section indicated: in this example, 21 CFR 880.2920 . It describes the device and says it is Class II. Once you have identified the correct classification regulation go to What are the Classification Panels below and click on the correct classification regulation or go to the CFR Search page. Elizabeth Bierman and Michele L. Buenafe, Morgan, Lewis & Bockius LLP Even as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) finalized its long-awaited guidance on mobile medical applications (or apps), wearable medical technology has emerged as a growing trend, presenting a new challenge for both the regulated industry and regulators. While this trend initially focused on wearables to monitor fitness, there already has been a natural progression towards development of technology that captures other physiologic information. Novel wearable devices under development that were featured at the 2014 Consumer Electronics Show and similar venues included, for example: * wrist bands to monitor heart rate and calories burned; * contact lenses to monitor glucose/insulin levels; * tee shirts that monitor heart rate, respiration rate, and skin temperature; * patches to monitor cardiac arrhythmias; * electroencephalography (EEG) headsets to monitor brain activity; and * "onesies" to monitor respiration in infants. Other innovative wearable products on the horizon may include sensors that monitor how often a person coughs, identify and track erratic behavior, and even provide advance warning of heart attacks. Wearable cameras may be used to help read laboratory test results. Because many wearables will involve new and unique technologies, they will present different regulatory challenges for companies seeking to develop and market these innovative devices, as well as for the FDA, which is responsible for regulating medical devices. Thus far, in the health IT area, the FDA has tackled the issue of remote display of information from medical devices (referred to as "medical device data systems" or MDDS) and mobile medical apps, which are software programs that can be run on a mobile phone, tablet computer, or similar mobile platform. Although the wearables that are being developed for medical applications are mobile and may be accompanied by software apps to monitor and track the data collected, most wearable medical technology also will include hardware, such as sensors, to capture the desired physiological information. Wearables, therefore, are not just another mobile medical app. FDA's regulatory guidance on mobile medical apps may be informative when assessing regulatory strategies for wearable technologies, however, the analysis does not end there, as the FDA regulatory status of the hardware and other sensors must also be considered. In the final guidance, the FDA answered industry's concern by significantly expanding the category of apps that would not be subject to active regulation, on the basis that these apps presented only minimal risk to patients. Notwithstanding its decision to actively regulate only a subset of higher risk mobile medical apps, the FDA confirmed that all such products are within its regulatory authority. The Final Guidance defines a regulated "mobile medical app" as a mobile app that (1) meets the definition of a "device" in Section 201(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act)[2] and (2) is intended either to be used as an accessory to a "regulated medical device" or to transform a mobile platform into a "regulated medical device." fetched_contents.text: Wearables and Atrial Fibrillation: Advances in Detection, Clinical Impact, Ethical Concerns, and Future Perspectives Abstract Atrial fibrillation (AF), the most common cardiac arrhythmia, is associated with a significantly increased risk of stroke, heart failure, and mortality. Early diagnosis and management are crucial to mitigating these risks. Wearable devices such as smartwatches and fitness bands, enhanced by advanced artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms, offer a promising solution for early AF detection due to their accessibility, ease of use, and cost-effectiveness. Although the ability of these algorithms to identify AF has been authorized, critical questions remain about their integration into clinical practice, ethical implications, and long-term benefits. This review uniquely explores the intersection of wearable technology and AF management, providing a detailed analysis of current evidence, emerging trends, and the challenges associated with these innovations. Keywords: artificial intelligence in medicine, atrial fibrillation (af), atrial fibrillation management, smart watches, wearables Introduction and background Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a condition in which the electrical impulses in the atria become rapid and disorganized, overriding the heart's natural pacemaker, irregular baseline made up of "f" (fibrillation) waves discharging at a frequency of 350 to 600 beats/min. These electrical impulses are triggered from multiple areas within and around the atria, rather than from a single area like the sinus node. This disrupts proper heart rate control, resulting in irregular heartbeats [1,2]. The growing prevalence of AF is largely a reflection of increasing global life expectancy, which contributes to the aging of populations worldwide. However, their validation in this population is limited. Objective The objective of this paper was to assess HR accuracy and validity from 2 wearables, the Corsano CardioWatch bracelet and the Hexoskin smart shirt, in children attending the pediatric cardiology outpatient clinic, exploring factors that influence accuracy, the Hexoskin shirt’s arrhythmia detection efficacy, and patient satisfaction. Methods Children with an indication for 24-hour Holter monitoring were equipped with a 24-hour Holter electrocardiogram (ECG; gold standard), together with both wearables. HR accuracy was defined as the percentage of HRs within 10% of Holter values, and agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on BMI, age, and time of wearing, among other factors. The association between accelerometry (expressed in gravitational units, g) and HR accuracy was analyzed to assess the impact of bodily movement on measurement accuracy. A blinded pediatric cardiologist analyzed Hexoskin shirt data for rhythm classification. Patient satisfaction was measured using a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire. Results A total of 31 participants (mean age 13.2, SD 3.6 y; n=14, 45% female) and 36 participants (mean age 13.3, SD 3.9 y) were included for the CardioWatch and Hexoskin measurements, respectively. Mean accuracy was 84.8% (SD 8.7%) for the CardioWatch and 87.4% (SD 11%) for the Hexoskin shirt. Hexoskin shirt accuracy was notably higher in the first 12 hours (94.9%, SD 7.4%) compared to the latter 12 (80%, SD 16.7%; P<.001). Higher accuracy was observed at lower HRs (low vs high HR: CardioWatch: 90.9%, SD 9.3% vs 79%, SD 10.6%; P<.001 and Hexoskin shirt: 90.6%, SD 14% vs 84.5, SD 11.8%; P<.001). Hexoskin shirt bias: –1.1 BPM; 95% LoA −19.5 to 17.4). HR measurement accuracy declined during more intense bodily movements. Correct classification of the Hexoskin’s shirt rhythm recordings was achieved in 86% (31/36) of cases. Recently, wearable devices, defined as biosensors that can be worn on the body to monitor various health parameters [7], have become increasingly popular and show potential for the follow-up care of patients with heart conditions [8]. ## Mini-report on evidence quality and limitations for cardiovascular disease detection

The evidence base for wearable devices used in cardiovascular disease detection is mixed in quality and scope. The validation studies cited here are primarily prospective cohort studies and measurement-accuracy studies, which are useful for assessing device performance under controlled or semi-controlled conditions but are not the gold standard for clinical utility. One study validated heart-rate accuracy in children using a 24-hour Holter ECG as the gold standard, with 31 and 36 participants in the CardioWatch and Hexoskin groups, respectively [N4-F4]. Another study proposed a heart-rate variability (HRV)-based method for evaluating wearable accuracy [N4-R2], while a third study assessed Fitbit Inspire 3 accuracy during cardiopulmonary exercise [N4-R4]. These designs are informative but limited by relatively small sample sizes and narrow clinical contexts, which reduces generalizability to broader adult or diverse CVD populations [N4-R1][N4-F4].

A key limitation across these studies is that accuracy does not fully capture clinical utility. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study found good agreement with Holter readings overall, but performance declined with higher heart rates, more intense movement, and later wearing times [N4-F4]. This suggests calibration issues and environmental interference remain common. The same study also found that patient satisfaction was higher than Holter, which is relevant but not equivalent to clinical accuracy [N4-F4]. Another limitation is that many studies are limited to adult samples, while the pediatric study explicitly notes that validity in children cannot be extrapolated from adult data [N4-F4]. This matters because CVD risk and physiology differ by age, and wearable performance can vary accordingly [N4-F4].

False positives and false negatives are also important concerns. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study reported rhythm classification by a blinded pediatric cardiologist, indicating that arrhythmia detection is not perfect and requires human oversight [N4-F4]. A broader review on atrial fibrillation detection notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, but also emphasizes that improper use can cause harm and that ECG remains required to confirm AF [N3-F3]. This highlights that consumer-facing devices may generate signals that are clinically meaningful but not definitive.

On clinical utility versus consumer marketing claims, the evidence suggests a gap between what devices can do and what claims are justified. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance distinguishes low-risk products that promote healthy lifestyles from medical devices, and manufacturers can shift into medical-device territory if claims or presentation imply therapeutic benefit [N6-R3]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study itself concludes that wearables show promise in diagnostics, therapeutic monitoring, and patient safety, but also says further research is needed to address measurement inaccuracies and how to counteract them [N4-F4]. This aligns with the broader caution in the CVD literature that wearable data can support early detection and risk monitoring, but should not replace clinical evaluation [N3-F3].

Overall, the evidence quality is strongest for heart-rate and rhythm monitoring in specific populations, weaker for broader CVD risk assessment, and most limited when claims extend beyond measurement accuracy to diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment guidance [N4-R1][N4-F4][N3-F3].

## Mini-report on the vital signs monitored and their cardiovascular relevance

Wearable devices commonly monitor heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) as the most directly cardiovascularly relevant signals. The evidence here shows that wearables use optical sensors and PPG to measure heart rate, and that HRV is used as a metric to assess accuracy and evaluate wearable performance [N2-R5][N2-R2][N4-R2]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study used Holter ECG as the gold standard for heart-rate validation, showing that heart-rate accuracy is central to assessing whether a wearable can reliably capture physiological changes over time [N4-F4]. HRV is especially important because it reflects autonomic nervous system activity and is associated with cardiac rhythm stability, stress, recovery, and overall cardiovascular health [N2-R1][N2-R3].

ECG or ECG-like activity is another core cardiovascular biomarker. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study evaluated rhythm classification and found that the Hexoskin shirt could detect arrhythmia with reasonable accuracy [N4-F4]. A separate review notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can passively measure heart rate from the wrist using PPG and analyze pulse irregularity and variability, which makes them promising for early AF detection [N3-F3]. That same review also states that smartwatch algorithms can detect atrial fibrillation with high accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. This indicates that wearables are increasingly capable of ECG-like rhythm analysis, even though they do not replace traditional ECG for confirmation [N3-F3][N3-R3].

Blood pressure and oxygen saturation are also relevant cardiovascular biomarkers. The evidence on blood pressure estimation is more technical and less mature than heart-rate monitoring. One review explicitly states that PPG-based devices can estimate blood pressure and that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation, sleep staging, and pulse oximetry [N5-R4]. Another source notes that hyperspectral PPG allows precise calculation of continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R1], while a wearable study uses dual PPG sensors to detect cardiac output and pulse characteristics [N5-R2]. Oxygen saturation is similarly mentioned as a monitored parameter in consumer-grade wearables, though the evidence here is indirect rather than a detailed validation study [N2-R2].

Continuous versus intermittent monitoring capabilities are a major distinction. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study used 24-hour free-living monitoring, which is continuous, and compared it with Holter ECG [N4-F4]. A review emphasizes that wearable cardiovascular monitoring systems provide real-time, personalized, and noninvasive continuous data [N2-R1]. The same review also notes that PPG-based systems can support continuous monitoring of heart rate and rhythm [N2-R1][N5-R4]. In contrast, intermittent monitoring would imply less frequent sampling and is not strongly evidenced in the provided sources. The evidence therefore supports continuous monitoring as the standard for CVD-relevant wearables, especially for detecting rhythm changes and tracking long-term physiological patterns [N2-R1][N4-F4].

Taken together, the cardiovascularly relevant vital signs monitored by wearables are heart rate, HRV, ECG-like rhythm detection, blood pressure estimation, and oxygen saturation. Continuous monitoring is the dominant mode, but accuracy and reliability vary by device, physiology, and environmental conditions [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-F4][N5-R1][N5-R4].

## Mini-report on CVD-specific monitoring capabilities and device capabilities

### Atrial fibrillation and arrhythmia detection in wearables
Wearables are increasingly used to detect atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias. The evidence shows that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, with very high sensitivity and specificity in some cases [N3-R4]. A separate review states that smartwatches and fitness bands can passively measure heart rate using PPG and analyze pulse irregularity and variability, making them promising for early AF detection [N3-F3]. It also reports that a smartwatch algorithm detected AF with 96.1% accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. However, the same review emphasizes that ECG is still required to confirm the diagnosis of AF, and that the inclusion of smartwatches in AF diagnosis and management has not yet been established [N3-F3].

The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study adds device-specific evidence for arrhythmia detection. The Hexoskin shirt was analyzed by a blinded pediatric cardiologist for rhythm classification, and correct classification was achieved in 86% of cases [N4-F4]. This suggests that wearables can detect rhythm abnormalities, but performance depends on the device and the population being studied [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that wearable arrhythmia detection is still emerging, with promise but not yet fully validated for clinical decision-making [N3-F3][N3-R3].

### Blood pressure estimation techniques and reliability
Blood pressure estimation in wearables is based on PPG and related pulse characteristics, but the reliability is less established than heart-rate monitoring. One review states that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation and sleep staging, and that hyperspectral PPG can calculate continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R4][N5-R1]. Another study uses dual PPG sensors on the palmar and dorsal sides of the wrist to detect cardiac output and pulse-related features, implying that blood pressure estimation is being approached through multiple PPG-derived signals [N5-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not include detailed validation of accuracy or inter-device comparison across multiple wearables.

The reliability issue is clear from the CardioWatch and Hexoskin study, which found that HR accuracy declined with increasing bodily movement and higher heart rates [N4-F4]. This implies that blood pressure estimation, which also depends on motion artifact and signal quality, may face similar or even greater challenges in real-world use. The evidence also suggests that blood pressure estimation is still an active area of research rather than a fully mature clinical capability [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Oxygen saturation and other cardiovascular biomarkers
Oxygen saturation is mentioned as a monitored parameter in consumer-grade wearables, though the evidence here is more indirect than a detailed validation study [N2-R2]. The broader wearable literature indicates that PPG-based devices can also support pulse oximetry, which is closely related to oxygen saturation monitoring [N5-R4]. Oxygen saturation is a cardiovascular biomarker because it reflects oxygen delivery to tissues and can signal hypoxemia, heart failure, or other conditions that affect oxygen transport.

The evidence does not provide a comprehensive list of all cardiovascular biomarkers monitored by wearables, but it does support the inclusion of oxygen saturation alongside heart rate, HRV, and blood-pressure-related signals [N2-R2][N5-R4]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study itself focused mainly on heart rate and rhythm, while the AF-specific evidence highlights additional rhythm and pulse-based capabilities [N4-F4][N3-F3].

### Device-specific performance across wrist-worn and other wearables
Device-specific performance varies by form factor and sensor technology. Wrist-worn wearables, such as smartwatches and fitness bands, are the most common and widely studied. They use PPG and optical sensors to monitor heart rate and rhythm [N2-R5][N3-R3][N3-F3]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study shows that wristband and ECG-shirt formats can both be used in pediatric monitoring, but the ECG shirt may offer better rhythm detection in some cases [N4-F4]. The Hexoskin shirt’s arrhythmia classification achieved 86% correct classification [N4-F4], whereas the CardioWatch showed good Holter agreement but also performance degradation during movement and higher HRs [N4-F4].

Other wearables, such as shirts, patches, and devices with dual PPG sensors, are designed for different physiological capture points. The dual PPG approach on the wrist is explicitly used for cardiac output and pulse estimation [N5-R2], suggesting that device form and sensor placement can affect what is measurable. The evidence here does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison across all wearable types, but it does indicate that wrist-worn wearables dominate the market and are the most frequently studied, while other forms offer alternative monitoring approaches [N2-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

Overall, CVD-specific monitoring in wearables is strongest for arrhythmia and rhythm detection, with emerging support for blood pressure estimation and oxygen saturation. Device performance varies by form factor, with wrist-worn wearables being the most established, but also the most challenged by motion artifact and changing physiology [N3-R3][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

## Mini-report on how wearables are classified commercially and by intended use

### Main regulatory categories and how they differ by intended purpose
The evidence points to a classification system based on intended use and risk level. The FDA classifies medical devices into Class I, II, and III, with Class I being the lowest risk and Class III the highest [N1-F1]. Device classification depends on intended use and indications for use, and the device’s risk to the patient or user is a major factor [N1-F1]. The FDA also explains that devices are assigned to one of three regulatory classes based on the level of control necessary to assure safety and effectiveness [N1-R3]. The general controls, special controls, and premarket approval requirements differ by class, with Class III requiring a premarket approval application (PMA) unless the device is a preamendments device or substantially equivalent to such a device [N1-F1]. This framework shows that intended purpose and risk level directly determine regulatory classification.

### Common device classes such as general wellness vs medical device
A clear distinction exists between general wellness devices and medical devices. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance states that low-risk general wellness products are not regulated devices, while medical devices are regulated under the FD&C Act [N6-R4]. The guidance also explains that low-risk general wellness products are not classified as medical devices and are not subject to the same premarket review as medical devices [N6-R4]. The 2026 general-wellness policy further narrows regulation for low-risk trackers while leaving privacy and security issues unresolved [N6-R2]. This means that a product can shift from general wellness to medical device status depending on its intended use, claims, and presentation [N6-R3]. The evidence therefore supports the distinction between wellness-oriented products and medical devices, with the latter requiring more rigorous FDA oversight.

### What clinical claims are allowed under each category
The evidence indicates that clinical claims are much more limited for general wellness products than for medical devices. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance is intended to provide clarity on compliance policy for low-risk products that promote a healthy lifestyle [N6-R1]. It also notes that the first category of general-wellness intended uses involves claims about sustaining or offering general improvement to functions associated with general wellness [N6-R5]. This implies that wellness products can make broad, non-therapeutic claims about health improvement, but they cannot make claims that imply medical diagnosis, treatment, or cure [N6-R1][N6-R5].

In contrast, medical devices are subject to FDA clearance or approval and can make more specific clinical claims if they are substantiated. The FDA guidance on mobile medical apps and wearable medical technology explains that wearables are not just mobile medical apps but also include hardware sensors and may involve new and unique technologies [N1-F2]. The FDA’s mobile medical apps guidance says that some apps are actively regulated as medical devices, while others are subject to enforcement discretion or are not considered devices at all [N1-F2]. For wearables, the evidence suggests that the hardware and sensors themselves must be evaluated under the FDA’s medical device framework [N1-F2].

### FDA de novo and downclassifying pathways
The FDA provides a pathway for devices that may be novel or not clearly classified under existing Class I, II, or III devices. The evidence here notes that if a device is not clearly classified, the FDA may consider downclassifying it from Class III to Class II [N1-R4]. The de novo pathway is also referenced as an option for novel devices [N1-R4]. The FDA’s guidance on medical devices explains that device classification depends on intended use and indications for use, and that the risk posed by the device is a major factor in class assignment [N1-F1]. The Morgan Lewis PDF specifically states that the FDA may consider downclassifying a device from Class III to Class II if the intended use and risk profile justify it [N1-R4]. This pathway is important because it allows novel wearables to enter the market without requiring full PMA if the risk and evidence support a lower-class classification.

Overall, the classification system is intended use and risk driven. General wellness products are not regulated as medical devices, while medical devices are classified as Class I, II, or III and subject to different premarket requirements. Clinical claims are more constrained for general wellness products and more flexible for medical devices. Downclassifying and de novo pathways exist for devices that do not fit existing classifications or require novel regulatory treatment [N1-F1][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R5].

## 1) How commercially available wearable devices are classified

Wearable devices are classified by intended use and by risk, with the FDA’s classification system distinguishing Class I, Class II, and Class III medical devices based on the level of control needed to ensure safety and effectiveness [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Class I is the lowest risk, Class II is moderate, and Class III is the highest risk [N1-F1]. The device’s intended use and indications for use are central to classification, meaning that a product can shift from general wellness to medical device status depending on what it is marketed to do [N1-F1][N6-R3].

### General wellness vs medical device
The FDA distinguishes low-risk general wellness products from medical devices. General wellness products are not regulated as medical devices and are not subject to the same premarket review as medical devices [N6-R4]. The general-wellness guidance explains that low-risk general wellness products are not regulated devices and are intended to promote healthy lifestyles rather than to diagnose, treat, or cure disease [N6-R1][N6-R5]. In contrast, medical devices are classified under the FDA’s medical device framework and may require 510(k) clearance, premarket approval, or other regulatory pathways [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### Clinical claims allowed under each category
Clinical claims are much more constrained for general wellness products. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance states that low-risk general wellness products are intended to promote a healthy lifestyle and can make claims about sustaining or offering general improvement to functions associated with general wellness [N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means they can make broad wellness claims, but they cannot make claims that imply medical diagnosis, treatment, or cure [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Medical devices, by contrast, may make more specific clinical claims if substantiated by evidence, but those claims still depend on the device’s classification and intended use [N1-F1][N6-R3].

### FDA de novo and downclassifying pathways
For devices that may be novel or not clearly classified, the FDA provides a de novo pathway and downclassifying pathways. The evidence notes that the FDA may consider downclassifying a device from Class III to Class II if the intended use and risk profile justify it [N1-R4]. The de novo pathway is also referenced as an option for novel devices [N1-R4]. This means that new wearables can enter the market through a different regulatory route if they do not fit existing classifications, but they still require FDA evaluation [N1-F1][N1-R4].

## 2) What vital signs wearables monitor and their cardiovascular relevance

Wearable devices commonly monitor heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV), which are among the most directly cardiovascularly relevant signals. The evidence shows that wearables use optical sensors and PPG to measure heart rate, and that HRV is used as a metric to assess accuracy and evaluate wearable performance [N2-R5][N2-R2][N4-R2]. Heart rate and HRV are central to detecting rhythm changes, stress, recovery, and overall cardiovascular health [N2-R1][N2-R3].

ECG or ECG-like activity is another core cardiovascular biomarker. The evidence indicates that wearables can analyze pulse irregularity and variability, making them promising for early atrial fibrillation detection [N3-F3]. A separate review reports that smartwatch algorithms can detect atrial fibrillation with 96.1% accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. It also notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, with very high sensitivity and specificity in some cases [N3-R4]. However, the same review emphasizes that ECG remains required to confirm the diagnosis of AF [N3-F3].

Blood pressure and oxygen saturation are also relevant cardiovascular biomarkers. The evidence on blood pressure estimation is more technical and less mature than heart-rate monitoring. One review states that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation and that hyperspectral PPG can calculate continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R4][N5-R1]. Another study uses dual PPG sensors on the palmar and dorsal sides of the wrist to detect cardiac output and pulse-related features, suggesting that blood pressure estimation is being approached through multiple PPG-derived signals [N5-R2]. Continuous monitoring is the dominant mode for CVD-relevant wearables. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study used 24-hour free-living monitoring, which is continuous, and compared it with Holter ECG [N4-F4]. A review emphasizes that wearable cardiovascular monitoring systems provide real-time, personalized, and noninvasive continuous data [N2-R1]. The same review also notes that PPG-based systems can support continuous monitoring of heart rate and rhythm [N2-R1][N5-R4]. In contrast, intermittent monitoring would imply less frequent sampling and is not strongly evidenced in the provided sources [N2-R1][N4-F4].

## 3) What CVD-specific monitoring capabilities wearables have

### Atrial fibrillation and arrhythmia detection
Wearables are increasingly used to detect atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias. The evidence shows that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, with very high sensitivity and specificity in some cases [N3-R4]. A separate review states that smartwatches and fitness bands can passively measure heart rate using PPG and analyze pulse irregularity and variability, making them promising for early AF detection [N3-F3]. It also reports that a smartwatch algorithm detected AF with 96.1% accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. However, the review also emphasizes that ECG is still required to confirm the diagnosis of AF, and that the inclusion of smartwatches in AF diagnosis and management has not yet been established [N3-F3].

The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study adds device-specific evidence for arrhythmia detection. The Hexoskin shirt was analyzed by a blinded pediatric cardiologist for rhythm classification, and correct classification was achieved in 86% of cases [N4-F4]. This suggests that wearables can detect rhythm abnormalities, but performance depends on the device and the population being studied [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that wearable arrhythmia detection is still emerging, with promise but not yet fully validated for clinical decision-making [N3-F3][N3-R3].

Blood pressure estimation in wearables is based on PPG and related pulse characteristics, but the reliability is less established than heart-rate monitoring. One review states that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation and sleep staging, and that hyperspectral PPG can calculate continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R4][N5-R1]. Another study uses dual PPG sensors on the palmar and dorsal sides of the wrist to detect cardiac output and pulse-related features, implying that blood pressure estimation is being approached through multiple PPG-derived signals [N5-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not include detailed validation of accuracy or inter-device comparison across multiple wearables.

The reliability issue is clear from the CardioWatch and Hexoskin study, which found that heart-rate accuracy declined with increasing bodily movement and higher heart rates [N4-F4]. This implies that blood pressure estimation, which also depends on motion artifact and signal quality, may face similar or even greater challenges in real-world use. The evidence also suggests that blood pressure estimation is still an active area of research rather than a fully mature clinical capability [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

Oxygen saturation is mentioned as a monitored parameter in consumer-grade wearables, though the evidence here is more indirect than a detailed validation study [N2-R2]. The evidence does not provide a comprehensive list of all cardiovascular biomarkers monitored by wearables, but it does support the inclusion of oxygen saturation alongside heart rate, HRV, and blood-pressure-related signals [N2-R2][N5-R4]. ## 4) Device-specific performance across wrist-worn and other wearables

Device-specific performance varies by form factor and sensor technology. Wrist-worn wearables, such as smartwatches and fitness bands, are the most common and widely studied. ## 5) Evidence quality and limitations for cardiovascular disease detection

The evidence base for wearable devices used in cardiovascular disease detection is mixed in quality and scope. The validation studies cited here are primarily prospective cohort studies and measurement-accuracy studies, which are useful for assessing device performance under controlled or semi-controlled conditions but are not the gold standard for clinical utility [N4-R1][N4-F4]. One study validated heart-rate accuracy in children using a 24-hour Holter ECG as the gold standard, with 31 and 36 participants in the CardioWatch and Hexoskin groups, respectively [N4-F4]. Another study proposed a heart-rate variability (HRV)-based method for evaluating wearable accuracy [N4-R2], while a third study assessed Fitbit Inspire 3 accuracy during cardiopulmonary exercise [N4-R4]. These designs are informative but limited by relatively small sample sizes and narrow clinical contexts, which reduces generalizability to broader adult or diverse CVD populations [N4-R1][N4-F4].

A key limitation across these studies is that accuracy does not fully capture clinical utility. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study found good agreement with Holter readings overall, but performance declined with higher heart rates, more intense movement, and later wearing times [N4-F4]. This suggests calibration issues and environmental interference remain common. The same study also found that patient satisfaction was higher than Holter, which is relevant but not equivalent to clinical accuracy [N4-F4]. Another limitation is that many studies are limited to adult samples, while the pediatric study explicitly notes that validity in children cannot be extrapolated from adult data [N4-F4]. This matters because CVD risk and physiology differ by age, and wearable performance can vary accordingly [N4-F4].

False positives and false negatives are also important concerns. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study reported rhythm classification by a blinded pediatric cardiologist, indicating that arrhythmia detection is not perfect and requires human oversight [N4-F4]. A broader review on atrial fibrillation detection notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, but also emphasizes that improper use can cause harm and that ECG remains required to confirm AF [N3-F3]. This highlights that consumer-facing devices may generate signals that are clinically meaningful but not definitive.

On clinical utility versus consumer marketing claims, the evidence suggests a gap between what devices can do and what claims are justified. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance distinguishes low-risk products that promote a healthy lifestyle from medical devices, and manufacturers can shift into medical-device territory if claims or presentation imply therapeutic benefit [N6-R3]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study itself concludes that wearables show promise in diagnostics, therapeutic monitoring, and patient safety, but also says further research is needed to address measurement inaccuracies and how to counteract them [N4-F4]. This aligns with the broader caution in the CVD literature that wearable data can support early detection and risk monitoring, but should not replace clinical evaluation [N3-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Commercially available wearable devices are classified by intended use and risk, with general wellness products generally not regulated as medical devices and medical devices classified as Class I, II, or III [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. Wearables can monitor heart rate, HRV, ECG-like activity, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation, with continuous monitoring being the standard mode for CVD-relevant signals [N2-R5][N2-R2][N2-R1][N5-R4]. For cardiovascular disease detection, wearables are especially useful for arrhythmia and AF detection, but evidence quality is mixed, and limitations such as false positives, false negatives, calibration issues, and small sample sizes remain [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Device performance also varies by form factor, with wrist-worn wearables being the most established, but also the most challenged by motion artifact and changing physiology [N3-R3][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

In short, wearables are useful for cardiovascular monitoring, but their clinical utility depends on evidence, regulatory classification, and realistic expectations about what they can reliably detect [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F3][N4-F4].

## Mini-report on evidence quality and limitations for cardiovascular disease detection

The evidence base for wearable devices used in cardiovascular disease detection is mixed in quality and scope. The validation studies cited here are primarily prospective cohort studies and measurement-accuracy studies, which are useful for assessing device performance under controlled or semi-controlled conditions but are not the gold standard for clinical utility. One study validated heart-rate accuracy in children using a 24-hour Holter ECG as the gold standard, with 31 and 36 participants in the CardioWatch and Hexoskin groups, respectively [N4-F4]. Another study proposed a heart-rate variability (HRV)-based method for evaluating wearable accuracy [N4-R2], while a third study assessed Fitbit Inspire 3 accuracy during cardiopulmonary exercise [N4-R4]. These designs are informative but limited by relatively small sample sizes and narrow clinical contexts, which reduces generalizability to broader adult or diverse CVD populations [N4-R1][N4-F4].

A key limitation across these studies is that accuracy does not fully capture clinical utility. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study found good agreement with Holter readings overall, but performance declined with higher heart rates, more intense movement, and later wearing times [N4-F4]. This suggests calibration issues and environmental interference remain common. The same study also found that patient satisfaction was higher than Holter, which is relevant but not equivalent to clinical accuracy [N4-F4]. A clear distinction exists between general wellness devices and medical devices. The guidance also explains that low-risk general wellness products are not classified as medical devices and are not subject to the same premarket review as medical devices [N6-R4]. This means that a product can shift from general wellness to medical device status depending on its intended use, claims, and presentation [N6-R3]. The evidence therefore supports the distinction between wellness-oriented products and medical devices, with the latter requiring more rigorous FDA oversight.

### What clinical claims are allowed under each category
The evidence indicates that clinical claims are much more limited for general wellness products than for medical devices. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance is intended to provide clarity on compliance policy for low-risk products that promote a healthy lifestyle [N6-R1]. It also notes that the first category of general-wellness intended uses involves claims about sustaining or offering general improvement to functions associated with general wellness [N6-R5]. This implies that wellness products can make broad, non-therapeutic claims about health improvement, but they cannot make claims that imply medical diagnosis, treatment, or cure [N6-R1][N6-R5].

The FDA provides a pathway for devices that may be novel or not clearly classified under existing Class I, II, or III devices. # Integrated final answer: How commercially available wearable devices are classified and what vital signs they monitor for cardiovascular disease detection

## 1) How commercially available wearable devices are classified

Wearable devices are classified by intended use and by risk, with the FDA’s classification system distinguishing Class I, Class II, and Class III medical devices based on the level of control needed to ensure safety and effectiveness [N1-F1][N1-R3]. Class I is the lowest risk, Class II is moderate, and Class III is the highest risk [N1-F1]. The device’s intended use and indications for use are central to classification, meaning that a product can shift from general wellness to medical device status depending on what it is marketed to do [N1-F1][N6-R3].

### General wellness vs medical device
The FDA distinguishes low-risk general wellness products from medical devices. General wellness products are not regulated as medical devices and are not subject to the same premarket review as medical devices [N6-R4]. The general-wellness guidance explains that low-risk general wellness products are not regulated devices and are intended to promote healthy lifestyles rather than to diagnose, treat, or cure disease [N6-R1][N6-R5]. In contrast, medical devices are classified under the FDA’s medical device framework and may require 510(k) clearance, premarket approval, or other regulatory pathways [N1-F1][N1-R4].

### Clinical claims allowed under each category
Clinical claims are much more constrained for general wellness products. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance states that low-risk general wellness products are intended to promote a healthy lifestyle and can make claims about sustaining or offering general improvement to functions associated with general wellness [N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means they can make broad wellness claims, but they cannot make claims that imply medical diagnosis, treatment, or cure [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Medical devices, by contrast, may make more specific clinical claims if substantiated by evidence, but those claims still depend on the device’s classification and intended use [N1-F1][N6-R3].

### FDA de novo and downclassifying pathways
For devices that may be novel or not clearly classified, the FDA provides a de novo pathway and downclassifying pathways. The evidence notes that the FDA may consider downclassifying a device from Class III to Class II if the intended use and risk profile justify it [N1-R4]. The de novo pathway is also referenced as an option for novel devices [N1-R4]. This means that new wearables can enter the market through a different regulatory route if they do not fit existing classifications, but they still require FDA evaluation [N1-F1][N1-R4].

## 2) What vital signs wearables monitor and their cardiovascular relevance

Wearable devices commonly monitor heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV), which are among the most directly cardiovascularly relevant signals. The evidence shows that wearables use optical sensors and PPG to measure heart rate, and that HRV is used as a metric to assess accuracy and evaluate wearable performance [N2-R5][N2-R2][N4-R2]. Heart rate and HRV are central to detecting rhythm changes, stress, recovery, and overall cardiovascular health [N2-R1][N2-R3].

ECG or ECG-like activity is another core cardiovascular biomarker. The evidence indicates that wearables can analyze pulse irregularity and variability, making them promising for early atrial fibrillation detection [N3-F3]. A separate review reports that smartwatch algorithms can detect atrial fibrillation with 96.1% accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. It also notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, with very high sensitivity and specificity in some cases [N3-R4]. However, the same review emphasizes that ECG remains required to confirm the diagnosis of AF [N3-F3].

Blood pressure and oxygen saturation are also relevant cardiovascular biomarkers. The evidence on blood pressure estimation is more technical and less mature than heart-rate monitoring. One review states that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation and that hyperspectral PPG can calculate continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R4][N5-R1]. Another study uses dual PPG sensors on the palmar and dorsal sides of the wrist to detect cardiac output and pulse-related features, suggesting that blood pressure estimation is being approached through multiple PPG-derived signals [N5-R2]. Oxygen saturation is mentioned as a monitored parameter in consumer-grade wearables, though the evidence here is more indirect than a detailed validation study [N2-R2].

### Continuous vs intermittent monitoring capabilities
Continuous monitoring is the dominant mode for CVD-relevant wearables. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study used 24-hour free-living monitoring, which is continuous, and compared it with Holter ECG [N4-F4]. A review emphasizes that wearable cardiovascular monitoring systems provide real-time, personalized, and noninvasive continuous data [N2-R1]. The same review also notes that PPG-based systems can support continuous monitoring of heart rate and rhythm [N2-R1][N5-R4]. In contrast, intermittent monitoring would imply less frequent sampling and is not strongly evidenced in the provided sources [N2-R1][N4-F4].

## 3) What CVD-specific monitoring capabilities wearables have

### Atrial fibrillation and arrhythmia detection
Wearables are increasingly used to detect atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias. The evidence shows that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, with very high sensitivity and specificity in some cases [N3-R4]. A separate review states that smartwatches and fitness bands can passively measure heart rate using PPG and analyze pulse irregularity and variability, making them promising for early AF detection [N3-F3]. It also reports that a smartwatch algorithm detected AF with 96.1% accuracy using 1-minute PPG recordings [N3-R3]. However, the review also emphasizes that ECG is still required to confirm the diagnosis of AF, and that the inclusion of smartwatches in AF diagnosis and management has not yet been established [N3-F3].

The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study adds device-specific evidence for arrhythmia detection. The Hexoskin shirt was analyzed by a blinded pediatric cardiologist for rhythm classification, and correct classification was achieved in 86% of cases [N4-F4]. This suggests that wearables can detect rhythm abnormalities, but performance depends on the device and the population being studied [N4-F4]. The evidence also indicates that wearable arrhythmia detection is still emerging, with promise but not yet fully validated for clinical decision-making [N3-F3][N3-R3].

### Blood pressure estimation techniques and reliability
Blood pressure estimation in wearables is based on PPG and related pulse characteristics, but the reliability is less established than heart-rate monitoring. One review states that PPG is used for blood pressure estimation and sleep staging, and that hyperspectral PPG can calculate continuous arteriolar pulse transit time for blood pressure estimation [N5-R4][N5-R1]. Another study uses dual PPG sensors on the palmar and dorsal sides of the wrist to detect cardiac output and pulse-related features, implying that blood pressure estimation is being approached through multiple PPG-derived signals [N5-R2]. However, the provided evidence does not include detailed validation of accuracy or inter-device comparison across multiple wearables.

The reliability issue is clear from the CardioWatch and Hexoskin study, which found that heart-rate accuracy declined with increasing bodily movement and higher heart rates [N4-F4]. This implies that blood pressure estimation, which also depends on motion artifact and signal quality, may face similar or even greater challenges in real-world use. The evidence also suggests that blood pressure estimation is still an active area of research rather than a fully mature clinical capability [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

### Oxygen saturation and other cardiovascular biomarkers
Oxygen saturation is mentioned as a monitored parameter in consumer-grade wearables, though the evidence here is more indirect than a detailed validation study [N2-R2]. The broader wearable literature indicates that PPG-based devices can also support pulse oximetry, which is closely related to oxygen saturation monitoring [N5-R4]. Oxygen saturation is a cardiovascular biomarker because it reflects oxygen delivery to tissues and can signal hypoxemia, heart failure, or other conditions that affect oxygen transport.

The evidence does not provide a comprehensive list of all cardiovascular biomarkers monitored by wearables, but it does support the inclusion of oxygen saturation alongside heart rate, HRV, and blood-pressure-related signals [N2-R2][N5-R4]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study itself focused mainly on heart rate and rhythm, while the AF-specific evidence highlights additional rhythm and pulse-based capabilities [N4-F4][N3-F3].

## 4) Device-specific performance across wrist-worn and other wearables

Device-specific performance varies by form factor and sensor technology. Wrist-worn wearables, such as smartwatches and fitness bands, are the most common and widely studied. They use PPG and optical sensors to monitor heart rate and rhythm [N2-R5][N3-R3][N3-F3]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study shows that wristband and ECG-shirt formats can both be used in pediatric monitoring, but the ECG shirt may offer better rhythm detection in some cases [N4-F4]. The Hexoskin shirt’s arrhythmia classification achieved 86% correct classification [N4-F4], whereas the CardioWatch showed good Holter agreement but also performance degradation during movement and higher HRs [N4-F4].

Other wearables, such as shirts, patches, and devices with dual PPG sensors, are designed for different physiological capture points. The dual PPG approach on the wrist is explicitly used for cardiac output and pulse estimation [N5-R2], suggesting that device form and sensor placement can affect what is measurable. The evidence here does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison across all wearable types, but it does indicate that wrist-worn wearables dominate the market and are the most frequently studied, while other forms offer alternative monitoring approaches [N2-R2][N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R4].

## 5) Evidence quality and limitations for cardiovascular disease detection

The evidence base for wearable devices used in cardiovascular disease detection is mixed in quality and scope. The validation studies cited here are primarily prospective cohort studies and measurement-accuracy studies, which are useful for assessing device performance under controlled or semi-controlled conditions but are not the gold standard for clinical utility [N4-R1][N4-F4]. One study validated heart-rate accuracy in children using a 24-hour Holter ECG as the gold standard, with 31 and 36 participants in the CardioWatch and Hexoskin groups, respectively [N4-F4]. Another study proposed a heart-rate variability (HRV)-based method for evaluating wearable accuracy [N4-R2], while a third study assessed Fitbit Inspire 3 accuracy during cardiopulmonary exercise [N4-R4]. These designs are informative but limited by relatively small sample sizes and narrow clinical contexts, which reduces generalizability to broader adult or diverse CVD populations [N4-R1][N4-F4].

A key limitation across these studies is that accuracy does not fully capture clinical utility. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study found good agreement with Holter readings overall, but performance declined with higher heart rates, more intense movement, and later wearing times [N4-F4]. This suggests calibration issues and environmental interference remain common. The same study also found that patient satisfaction was higher than Holter, which is relevant but not equivalent to clinical accuracy [N4-F4]. Another limitation is that many studies are limited to adult samples, while the pediatric study explicitly notes that validity in children cannot be extrapolated from adult data [N4-F4]. This matters because CVD risk and physiology differ by age, and wearable performance can vary accordingly [N4-F4].

False positives and false negatives are also important concerns. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study reported rhythm classification by a blinded pediatric cardiologist, indicating that arrhythmia detection is not perfect and requires human oversight [N4-F4]. A broader review on atrial fibrillation detection notes that smartwatches and fitness bands can detect arrhythmias independently of ECG checks when patients are free of symptoms, but also emphasizes that improper use can cause harm and that ECG remains required to confirm AF [N3-F3]. This highlights that consumer-facing devices may generate signals that are clinically meaningful but not definitive.

On clinical utility versus consumer marketing claims, the evidence suggests a gap between what devices can do and what claims are justified. The FDA’s general-wellness guidance distinguishes low-risk products that promote a healthy lifestyle from medical devices, and manufacturers can shift into medical-device territory if claims or presentation imply therapeutic benefit [N6-R3]. The CardioWatch and Hexoskin study itself concludes that wearables show promise in diagnostics, therapeutic monitoring, and patient safety, but also says further research is needed to address measurement inaccuracies and how to counteract them [N4-F4]. This aligns with the broader caution in the CVD literature that wearable data can support early detection and risk monitoring, but should not replace clinical evaluation [N3-F3].

## 6) Bottom line

Commercially available wearable devices are classified by intended use and risk, with general wellness products generally not regulated as medical devices and medical devices classified as Class I, II, or III [N1-F1][N1-R3][N6-R1]. Wearables can monitor heart rate, HRV, ECG-like activity, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation, with continuous monitoring being the standard mode for CVD-relevant signals [N2-R5][N2-R2][N2-R1][N5-R4]. For cardiovascular disease detection, wearables are especially useful for arrhythmia and AF detection, but evidence quality is mixed, and limitations such as false positives, false negatives, calibration issues, and small sample sizes remain [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Device performance also varies by form factor, with wrist-worn wearables being the most established, but also the most challenged by motion artifact and changing physiology [N3-R3][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

In short, wearables are useful for cardiovascular monitoring, but their clinical utility depends on evidence, regulatory classification, and realistic expectations about what they can reliably detect [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-F3][N4-F4].
